articles.title_orig: Dow slides weighed by Home Depot; Nasdaq is flat ahead of Nvidia earnings: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow slides weighed by Home Depot; Nasdaq is flat ahead of Nvidia earnings: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stocks dropped on Tuesday, pressured by renewed selling in semiconductor names, as traders braced for Nvidia's much-anticipated earnings report.
A CNN story about a National Security Agency network outage added to recent jitters about the country's technology infrastructure and helped weigh on the market, traders said.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 741 points, or 1.4%. The Nasdaq Composite lost 1%, while the S&P 500 slipped 1%. The Dow was down 900 points at its low.
Major averages fell to their lows of the session following the report from CNN that said a classified network used by the NSA had gone down, citing people familiar with the matter. CNN's sources said there was no evidence that it was a cyberattack.
Traders said the report helped take equities lower, though the losses were contained. This reported outage is latest in a string of incidents that have left people on edge including the FAA groundstop over the weekend, Microsoft's Outlook outage last week and some recent issues with banking apps.
Nvidia shares trades off their lows of the session after former CEO Jensen Huang said he would be open to returning as CEO if the company's board thought that was in the best interest of shareholders. Traders are on edge ahead of the chipmaker's earnings after the bell.
Despite Nvidia's share comeback, the rest of technology was lower with Micron Technology sliding roughly 6%. Advanced Micro Devices slipped more than 1.5%, while Intel was down 4% and Marvell Technology shed more than 2%.
Microsoft shares were down 3% and among the biggest tech lowers.
Neocloud stocks CoreWeave and Iren shed 5% and 6%, respectively. Nebius lost 4.2%. Investor Steve Eisman told CNBC earlier in the day that these stocks had the most to lose if the Huang scandal causes Nvidia to pull back its financing of the AI ecosystem.
Investor Steve Eisman said AI neocloud stocks will sustain the biggest losses in the ongoing Nvidia scandal.
Nvidia was essentially a "virtual vertical holding company and it's unwinding," said Eisman of "Big Short" fame on CNBC's "Squawk Box ." "I think neoclouds are all in big trouble though because they are part of that vertical holding company and I think they're about to get ejected."
CoreWeave and Nebius are down about 4% and 2% on the day, respectively.
Neoclouds, which used borrowed funds to build data centers, have been among the hardest-hit stocks during the recent pullback in the artificial intelligence trade.
— Tobias Burns, Liz Napolitano
China Internet ETF (KWEB) hits its lowest level on Tuesday since November 2022, sending the fund's performance down more than 33% year-to-date. That took several large Chinese stocks to fresh lows.
Shares of Kingsoft Cloud, a company that sells cloud services, are down nearly 7%, reaching a 52-week low of $6.41 per share.
Shares of Bilibili, the major Chinese online entertainment and video platform, are down 4.3%, reaching a 52-week low of $12.
And shares of Alibaba, the ecommerce and tech company, fell nearly 3%, also reaching a 52-week low of $87 per share.
The Home Depot 's stock is under pressure despite the home improvement chain beating on both earnings and revenue and posting its strongest same-store sales growth in four years.
Shares of the retailer slipped nearly 3% on Tuesday.
Likely weighing on shares is the company's conservative implied outlook for the holiday season quarter amid ongoing housing headwinds and a cautious consumer environment.
Home Depot said it expects full-year adjusted EPS rising 2% from last year's $14.69 – leading to a projected EPS figure of $14.98 for this year. But after posting a 10-cent beat in the third quarter, that full-year projection implies fourth quarter adjusted EPS of $2.77 – solidly below the current consensus estimate of $2.81.
The retailer's same-store sales forecast is also underwhelming. Despite a slight beat in the just-completed quarter (up 2.2% vs. the Street's estimate of up 1.8%), Home Depot's projection of 1.4% same-store sales growth for this year is a hair below Wall Street's expectation for 1.5% growth.
U.S. equities were trading lower shortly after the opening bell on Tuesday.
The S&P 500 was down 0.3%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.6%, or 303 points. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite edged down 0.2%
Anthropic is likely to price its initial public offering above its proposed range of $70 to $78 a share, multiple sources told CNBC's David Faber on Tuesday.
The artificial intelligence company plans to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Nov. 19 under the ticker "ANT." The final offer price has yet to be set, according to CNBC's report .
St. Louis Federal Reserve President Alberto Musalem indicated Tuesday that the central bank may need as many as four rate hikes in coming months, offering one of the most hawkish views yet by a Fed policymaker about the steps needed to quell inflation.
During a speech delivered in Argentina, Musalem made the case that current policy is not significantly restricting economic activity.
"The economy will likely require several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027 to achieve 2% inflation in a timely manner," he said.
Read the full story below.
Spending in the retail sector rose 0.2% in October, matching expectations, though the ex-autos figure came in higher than forecast, the Commerce Department reported Tuesday.
A 1.6% decline in motor vehicle and parts sales held back the headline number, while a 4.7% surge in miscellaneous retailers helped offset other soft areas. Sales at gasoline stations rose 1.5% despite a general easing in energy prices.
In other economic news Tuesday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that import prices increased 1.1%, higher than the 0.7% estimate.
Nvidia reports earnings after the bell, and big investors may have shied away from it ahead of the release.
Morgan Stanley analyst Erik Woodring noted that Nvidia "was the most 'under-owned' large-cap tech stock exiting the quarter."
"NVDA remained the most under-owned large-cap tech stock we track as of 3Q26 end, with the gap between NVDA's S&P 500 weighting and institutional ownership widening Q/Q by 22bps, ending 3Q26 at -2.75%, an all-time high. However, given NVDA shares have fallen 32% in the last 45 days vs. AAPL up 6%, it's highly plausible Apple could be the most under-owned mega-cap tech stock at present," he said.
The European Union's executive body on Tuesday upgraded its growth forecasts for the bloc, attributing an "upward surprise" across the first three quarters to a rebound in exports and solid consumption.
The European Commission's autumn report forecast euro area economic expansion of 1.4% in 2026, up from 1.1% in its spring forecast, followed by 1.4% growth in 2027, in line with its previous forecast.
That was despite a forecast of higher inflation pressures in the 21-nation euro area, estimated to hit an average 3.2% in 2026 and 3.1% in 2027, versus prior estimates of 3% and 2.2%. Euro zone inflation was 4% in October.
Energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz remain "severely disrupted," while freight and insurance costs have risen sharply, and bottlenecks in refining capacity and tight gas markets have all contributed to price pressures, the report said.
However, it said that medium-term inflation expectations were "well anchored," with markets remaining confident in the European Central Bank's ability to maintain price stability following 25 basis point rate hikes in June and September.
Rate hikes by central banks globally, rising government bond yields, uncertain trade policy, volatile stock markets and "concerns about the profitability and financing of AI companies" are all influencing the global economy, which is nonetheless continuing to expand amid strong growth in AI-related investment, it said.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia's Huang signals willingness to return as CEO; board creates national security panel
articles.title_zh: Nvidia's Huang signals willingness to return as CEO; board creates national security panel
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang broke his silence after resigning from the company following revelations of multiple affairs, saying he'd be willing to return as its CEO.
"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life," Huang said in a statement Tuesday morning. "I created problems for the board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the board's independent investigation."
Nvidia board members are not interested in reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO or in any other role at the chipmaker, a source directly familiar with their thinking told CBS News. More than 190,000 people, including several thousand Nvidia employees, have signed a petition to reinstate Huang.
"If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," he said.
— This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.
Caitlin  Yilek contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Putin's Crimea bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Putin's Crimea bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridge
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.
The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack.
Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - had been closed after Russia hit Ukraine's capital overnight.
The Southern bridge partially reopened on Tuesday, Klitschko said.
Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.
While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.
The Crimean Bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014.
The $3.6bn (Â£2.7bn) piece of infrastructure is widely seen in Russia and Ukraine as Putin's personal pet project: His close tycoon friend Arkady Rotenberg built it, and then Putin personally opened it by driving a lorry over it in May 2018.
In Ukraine, the much-hated bridge is seen as one of the main symbols of Russia's continuing occupation of Ukrainian lands.
Putin (centre) personally opened the Crimean Bridge by driving a lorry over it in May 2018
The damage after the overnight attack, involving cruise missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section of the bridge apparently destroyed.
Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.
Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".
He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".
The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and Russia's transport ministry later said some rail services resumed.
Ukraine's state security service SBU said its operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.
Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".
For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.
Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.
Watch: BBC reports from Kyiv bridge hit by Russian attack
Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies.
On Tuesday morning, Zelensky said four ballistic missiles had targeted the Southern Bridge, and another three had been fired on the Northern Bridge.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground metro services were also damaged in the overnight attacks, local officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River, connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Strikes on the busy Northern and Southern Bridges will cause major disruption to people's daily lives.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the central Cherkasy region, according to local officials.
The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear, though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.
The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia â at least until the crossing can be repaired.
However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.
This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.
Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge â particularly its enormous arch â may have blocked the shipping channel.
This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdyansk.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

articles.title_orig: Duffy wants $50 billion to avert another ground stop. Experts say money isn’t the issue.
articles.title_zh: Duffy wants $50 billion to avert another ground stop. Experts say money isn’t the issue.
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
An equipment upgrade appears to have brought airline departures across the U.S. to a standstill Friday , raising questions about how the nation’s air traffic control network is being modernized — and whether safeguards should have prevented the disruption.
The nationwide ground stop — the longest since the September 11 attacks — led to 14,000 flights cancellations Friday and Saturday as the disruption and its aftermath spread through airline schedules. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy initially blamed an “incredibly old air traffic control system,” saying communications equipment became “overloaded with data” and “went down.” By Saturday, he pointed more specifically to routine work replacing copper telecommunications wiring with fiber .
Aviation experts said precautions should have prevented an equipment change from overwhelming the network, leading to scrutiny over installation procedures and preparations for recovering when an upgrade goes wrong.
The disruption has also intensified a funding debate , with Duffy seeking another $50 billion after Congress approved $12.5 billion last year. But experts caution that new equipment alone cannot eliminate failures in a sprawling system that must remain operational throughout its overhaul.
“A large-scale modernization, no matter how warranted and well-intended, cannot solve all these problems. This is a system that runs 24/7, 365 days a year. We cannot turn it off while we build a new one and then start a new one from scratch,” David Lovell, a professor of civil and environmental engineering at the University of Maryland, told The Independent .
“Any modernization will, by necessity, be done piecemeal. That will mean integrating new subsystems with old subsystems, with the consequent interfaces at the boundaries that are often points of vulnerability,” he added.
Air traffic controllers began seeing inconsistencies in radar data and aircraft communications at 3:36 p.m. Friday, Duffy said. Eighteen minutes later, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop , barring departures as officials sought to identify the problem.
The order was lifted at 8:15 p.m., but airlines continued struggling to restore their schedules. More than 7,000 flights were canceled Friday, with thousands more canceled or delayed Saturday, leaving thousands of passengers stranded at airports across the U.S.
Duffy said Saturday that contractor L3Harris may have installed a faulty router — a device that directs information through a network — at a site in Arkansas . The work involved replacing copper wires, which carry electrical signals, with fiber optic cables, which can transmit more data over longer distances.
L3Harris has partnered with the federal government for a decade and is replacing the Federal Aviation Administration’s copper wires with fiber-optic cables. FAA and company officials are working in L3Harris’ Florida lab to analyze the router at the center of the stop.
“L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously,” the company said in a statement.
The company’s work comes the nation has long sought to upgrade its decade-old air traffic control system. Edward Booth, an aviation attorney and pilot based in Jacksonville, Florida, told Time Magazine that billions of dollars have already been sunk into the process.
“It's a very highly technical, robust system,” Booth says of the National Airspace System (NAS), “but it seems the weak spot was discovered yesterday afternoon.”
An overload can affect facilities around the country that exchange radar information and voice communications, said Hassan Shahidi, president and CEO of the Flight Safety Foundation.
“It appears to have been a system overload caused by this new router,” he told The Independent .
Lance Sherry, a professor of systems engineering at George Mason University, said air traffic control comprises three interacting networks: communications, navigation and surveillance. Their connections help explain how a local problem can spread to a nationwide shutdown.
“For this reason we consider [air traffic control] to be a network-of-networks,” Sherry said. “A perturbation in one location of the network can, under the right circumstances, propagate through the network.”
Independent industry analyst Bob Mann noted that the FAA had recently expanded its SMART traffic-management platform nationwide. The AI-assisted tool, which helps FAA staff plan traffic flows, was rolled out nationally three days before the ground stop.
Federal officials, however, have said this new tool was not responsible for the outage.
Lovell said the disruption should not obscure the safety response.
“The safety aspects of the system performed admirably,” he told The Independent . “The procedures to get aircraft out of the air safely worked perfectly, and there was no loss of life or bodily injury.”
The FAA and its telecommunications provider should have safeguards to prevent an equipment change from overwhelming the network, Shahidi said. Preliminary findings pointed to a router setting that apparently allowed it to send excessive information.
“This particular router has a feature that has a broader broadcast capability. That feature apparently was not disabled,” he said.
While investigators were still establishing the cause, he argued that appropriate settings, testing and training should block such an overload. “This is something that I believe is preventable,” he said.
The FAA has already replaced more than 3,500 copper communications lines with fiber-optic connections, out of 5,170 scheduled for replacement by 2028.
With many more upgrades ahead, Shahidi said understanding what went wrong and preparing for future installations is essential. “They need to have a plan, a backup plan,” he said.
The disruption has sharpened a dispute over whether the FAA needs more money or a better plan for spending what it already has. The administration says existing funding cannot cover a full overhaul, while Democrats are demanding an accounting of unspent money and a clearer explanation of what another $50 billion would buy.
Congress approved $12.5 billion for modernization last year, which Duffy has described as a down payment rather than the full cost of replacing outdated systems. By Friday, he increased that request to $50 billion, calling the need an “emergency.”
“This is bipartisan. This is American. I want $50 billion,” Duffy said Friday.
President Donald Trump took a more partisan approach in Sunday Truth Social posts, accusing the Biden administration of making an “ old and broken system worse than when they began .” He urged Congress to approve funding rather than modernizing in “drips and drabs.”
Democrats say their objections are not to modernization itself, but to the administration’s management of the effort. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, said previously approved funding largely remained unspent and accused Duffy of demanding “a $50 billion ransom without a real plan to deliver.”
“Congress has shown its willingness to modernize the FAA’s systems and support its workforce as part of annual bipartisan legislation, but we need a competent partner at the Department of Transportation to carry this out in a sustainable, transparent manner,” she said in a statement.
Beyond the funding dispute lies a separate question: whether replacing old equipment would prevent another disruption similar to Friday’s. Lovell said the suspected involvement of newly installed routers complicated that argument.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia's board forms export oversight panel after scrutiny over China chip sales
articles.title_zh: Nvidia's board forms export oversight panel after scrutiny over China chip sales
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia on Tuesday said its board has formed a committee to oversee its national security policies and compliance with U.S. export controls, a step that comes amid heightened scrutiny of the chipmaker's sales practices to some Southeast Asian companies.
The move comes days after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO over revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, as well as a subordinate at the company. The woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation), had worked for a Singapore-based data center company, Megaspeed, which had bought billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia chips.
Nvidia also faces mounting pressure in Washington, D.C., with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle expressing concern that China is gaining access to the company's advanced chips, which are critical to developing AI models. The U.S. has barred sales of Nvidia's highest-end chips to China due to national security and competitive concerns.
On Monday, the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim rule limiting other countries' access to advanced chips that power artificial intelligence.
Jensen Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter have agreed to appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence Committee, according to a statement on Tuesday from the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
"The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia's role in allowing dangerous [People's Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal," the committee chairs, Reps. Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, said in the statement.
Nvidia said its existing National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team will report directly to the new committee and its interim CEO, Colette Kress.
"Nvidia recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security," Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board of directors, said in a statement.
The company added that the decision to create the committee reflects the board's commitment "to demonstrate the highest standards of governance and oversight."
Nvidia shares have dropped 16% following news of Huang's extramarital relationships and his departure from the company, which has shed more than $700 billion in value in the wake of the scandal. Nvidia's business could also take a hit if new U.S. restrictions on sales of semiconductors and chipmaking equipment affect its sales to China, according to Wall Street analysts.
"Any new leadership will be very wary of drawing the ire of either the U.S. Congress or the U.S. Treasury and will consequently err on the side of caution when it comes to authorizing any non-U.S. sales," Louis-Vincent Gave, CEO of investment adviser Gavekal, said in a report.
The spotlight on Nvidia also comes at a delicate time for U.S.-China relations, especially as the countries compete in AI. President Trump arrived Tuesday in the Philippines to start a multiday swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with China's President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin later this week.
Chinese government officials warned the U.S. last week against imposing additional guardrails on chip exports, which China said would disrupt global supply chains.

articles.title_orig: Trump meets key US regional allies in Manila ahead of China visit
articles.title_zh: Trump meets key US regional allies in Manila ahead of China visit
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
GUANGZHOU, China — Behind the scenes, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spent months pushing for action that would signal resolve within the Trump administration against China’s pursuit of the most powerful American computer chips, a flashpoint in their race for superiority in artificial intelligence, multiple sources said.
But Trump’s courtship of Xi Jinping, seeking to alleviate tensions among the world’s greatest powers, and a contingent of advisors skeptical of commercial warfare against Beijing slowed the process down — giving China months of opportunity to gain access to U.S. semiconductors through the back door.
Ultimately, just hours before departing for Asia alongside President Trump, Bessent got his way, bolstering his position ahead of talks with Chinese officials in Shenzhen this week on the risks posed by frontier systems.
A new rule tightening loopholes in U.S. export controls sends a dual message to Beijing ahead of Thursday’s summit, that Washington is serious about curbing Chinese circumvention — and that China hawks within the administration may be gaining the upper hand.
Trump has repeatedly sidestepped confrontation with Xi over the intensifying AI race in their two previous meetings this year, in Beijing and Washington, wary of upsetting a carefully managed détente and reluctant to jeopardize a technology boom increasingly central to the U.S. economy.
The new rules restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best AI models.
But the administration, from the president down, is acutely aware of China’s ambitions to dominate an industry that could reshape the global balance of power. That competitive drive was underscored this month by a scandal involving a Chinese espionage campaign targeting Jensen Huang, co-founder of Nvidia, the world’s leading AI chip maker.
Before resigning from the company in disgrace over the weekend, Huang admitted to having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy — a woman who worked at a Singaporean firm accused by American authorities of helping to divert restricted Nvidia chips to China, in violation of U.S. export controls.
The national security scandal has roiled the markets — and in so doing, commanded Trump’s attention — inflicting a significant devaluation on Nvidia and reverberating well beyond it, wiping nearly $1 trillion from the combined market value of major technology companies in a single trading session on Monday.
Trump, who counts Huang a friend and ally, indicated he would be open to his return as Nvidia’s chief executive . Bessent suggested otherwise, expressing confidence its board could find competent new leadership and urging a full investigation.
Trump is not expected to raise the Nvidia matter directly with Xi. But Bessent plans to do so in his own meetings, one official said.
The Treasury secretary has thus taken on the role of an enforcer, pursuing a tougher line than Trump is willing to take himself in his highly personalized relationship with the Chinese leader.
Bessent is scheduled to meet with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng on the sidelines of the summitry in Shenzhen to discuss potential collaboration on AI safety protocols, standards for testing of advanced models, and a direct communications channel for AI emergencies.
The two men have met before to discuss AI, most recently in New York, where they agreed in principle to coordinate. But the talks have yet to produce much in the way of tangible results.
“Bessent is signaling that, while he sees working with Beijing to mitigate AI risks as a priority, it won’t come at the expense of actions that he sees as necessary to protect U.S. national security, like limiting AI chip exports to China,” said Daniel Remler, a senior fellow with the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a New American Security.
The administration’s latest action marks a policy defeat for Howard Lutnick , secretary of the Commerce Department, who oversees chip policy and had advocated for a less restrictive approach than Bessent, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Jamieson Greer, the U.S. trade representative.
The feud began spilling into public view ahead of the president’s travel, and in light of the Nvidia scandal, after Bessent said in a television interview that the Commerce Department “has the pen” to act, implying a split within the team.
“Look, there’re two different views,” Trump told reporters on Monday, answering questions on the matter. “One view is you don’t want to insult China. We have a very good relationship with China, and you don’t want to insult them.”
“The other view is just go, you know, down and dirty and do what you have to do,” Trump continued. “You can’t say either is wrong or right. We’ll let you know.”
Beyond the diplomatic niceties, Trump has been explicit and consistent since resuming office that the United States must “win” the race for AI superiority, calling the alternative “not acceptable.”
“Whoever wins AI,” Trump said at the UN General Assembly in September, “whoever wins superintelligence, wins.”
Trump will arrive in China on Wednesday after meeting with world leaders in Manila, including those from the Quad — an alliance of Japan, India, Australia and the United States — which discussed AI at their own summit Tuesday evening.
Describing “superintelligence” — Trump’s preferred term for AI — as “the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the industrial revolution,” Trump announced a Quad effort to accelerate adoption of the technology, including an investment of more than $85 million to enhance AI ecosystems throughout the region.
“We want to be careful with it,” Trump said, “but it’s amazing, the things that have come out, in terms of science and in terms of medical breakthroughs. No one can believe what we’re finding. And we’re finding it fast.”
“We want to be very careful, but we want to cherish it,” he added. “The United States as you know is leading in that capacity, by quite a bit.”
As he meets with the leaders of India, Japan and Australia, Trump will face pressure to sustain resolve against Beijing despite his yearlong courtship of President Xi Jinping.
The new U.S. rule requires overseas data centers serving customers in China, Russia, Iran and Cuba to identify their end users before gaining access to chips. It also imposes additional licensing requirements on chip sales to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, which the Commerce Department identifies as posing a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to unauthorized destinations.
U.S. officials say that export controls are not up for negotiation in talks with the Chinese. But Beijing sees them as yet another historic example of Washington trying to contain its rise — a posture that has repeatedly stifled diplomatic progress between the two superpowers.
“While administration officials say export controls aren’t up for negotiation, Chinese officials will certainly bring them up,” Remler said. “These restrictions are the key obstacle to China’s AI progress, which is increasingly important to the Chinese economy and to Xi’s strategic goals.”
China claims it does not seek an all-powerful, generalized “superintelligence,” but rather specialized AI systems embedded across industries to boost productivity and improve quality of life.
In Beijing’s telling, it is the United States — pursuing generalized AI through a private sector largely unchecked by the federal government — that poses an existential threat to the global order.
Sheila Jasanoff, a professor of science and technology studies at the Harvard Kennedy School, said China “has a much clearer vision of what it is seeking to accomplish in the so-called AI arms race, as well as the capacity to benefit from Nvidia’s

articles.title_orig: Trump’s trip to the Philippines and China in photos
articles.title_zh: Trump’s trip to the Philippines and China in photos
articles.content_orig:
David E. Sanger and Katie Rogers
President Trump landed in Manila on Tuesday to begin a 48-hour Asia trip in which he will meet with Xi Jinping of China and other world leaders, with an unpredictable agenda that could include the future of American tariffs, nuclear arms control, the war in Ukraine and U.S. restrictions on advanced A.I. chips.
Mr. Trump was scheduled to meet with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines and attend a gathering of Southeast Asian leaders. After less than 24 hours in Manila, he will head to the APEC economic summit in Shenzhen, China, where he was expected to meet with Mr. Xi and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.
The brief itinerary appears to reflect Mr. Trump’s preferences. He dislikes big summits where he often is not the sole subject of attention. And he enjoys meeting with leaders of powerful nations — especially Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin, two authoritarian leaders he often talks about in admiring terms.
Mr. Trump will be meeting Mr. Xi for the third time this year, and a three-way meeting between China, Russia and the United States would be the first of its kind.
On Tuesday, Mr. Trump caught the end of a dayslong meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN, after issuing tariffs on countries across the region, even allies. Those moves added to a sentiment in Asia that the United States was not a reliable partner but rather one that treasured its commercial interests over its security interests. The only event of substance on the president’s schedule on Tuesday — signing what he had called a “ trade deal ” with Thailand — did not happen because Mr. Trump said it was still being finalized.
Mr. Trump met with leaders from the so-called Quad — the United States, India, Japan and Australia — soon after his arrival. All three partners are smarting from high energy prices triggered by the Iran war, a conflict Mr. Trump never discussed with them before launching it in late February.
In Shenzhen — the heart of China’s robotics and artificial intelligence industries — Mr. Trump will pursue détente with Mr. Xi. He needs to extend a soon-expiring trade truce that limited tariffs on Chinese goods entering the United States in return for a Chinese commitment not to cut off rare earths and magnets.
Then comes the main event: the meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin. Referring to the trilateral meeting, Mr. Trump told reporters before leaving Washington: “We are going to be talking about denuclearization, a tough subject because it is very hard for any of us to say we’ll get rid of our nukes.” Chinese officials have made clear they are not interested in nuclear talks until their arsenal is roughly the size of the American one.
Mr. Trump also said, “We will talk about Iran a little,” insisting the situation was in “very good shape.” Analysts say it is unlikely that the meeting will make any progress on Iran, with Russia happy to see energy prices elevated since the war began, and China eager to see them rapidly decline.
Here’s what else we’re covering:
Protests: Thousands of demonstrators assembled in downtown Manila on Tuesday in opposition to Mr. Trump’s visit and to a U.S.-led initiative called Pax Silica, which aims to unite partners around A.I. supply chains independent of China. Read more ›
North Korea: Mr. Putin could meet with Kim Jong-un if the North Korean leader also travels to China for the APEC summit, Russian state news agencies reported, citing the Kremlin’s spokesman. It was not clear whether Mr. Kim would attend the summit.
Ukraine: Mr. Trump also said he would talk about Ukraine, on which Mr. Putin’s aides are engaging in talks with the U.S. and Ukrainian officials, but also renewing demands that NATO pull back its troops to where they were before the alliance expanded toward Russia.
President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia could meet with Kim Jong-un if the North Korean leader travels to China for the APEC summit this week, the Kremlin said, reflecting the deepening of ties between their countries in recent years.
Asked about the possibility of a meeting, Dmitri S. Peskov, the Kremlin spokesman, said on Monday that it would “of course” happen if Mr. Kim went to Shenzhen, the Chinese economic hub and host city, according to Russian state news agencies. North Korea has not confirmed whether Mr. Kim plans to attend the summit.
Mr. Putin and Mr. Kim have publicly met three times since 2022, and North Korea has been a key supporter of Russia’s military actions in Ukraine.
As the war in Ukraine nears its fifth anniversary, with no end in sight, the Kremlin is expected to use Mr. Putin’s many meetings at the APEC summit to showcase how Russia is regarded as one of the major international powers alongside the United States and China.
A visit by Mr. Kim would be a rare foray outside North Korea for the leader, and it would further raise the prospect that he could meet with President Trump in China. On the first day of his 48-hour trip to Asia, Mr. Trump told reporters that Mr. Kim “would like” to come to the APEC summit. The president has repeatedly said he would like to meet with Mr. Kim again.
On Wednesday, Mr. Putin is scheduled to meet with Xi Jinping, China’s leader. On Thursday, he is set to take part in a trilateral summit with Mr. Xi and Mr. Trump, the first meeting of its kind. The Kremlin said on Monday that it was working to arrange a bilateral meeting between Mr. Putin and Mr. Trump.
Before his departure for China, Mr. Putin met on Monday in the Kremlin with Jo Yong-won, a secretary of North Korea’s ruling Workers’ Party. During the meeting, Mr. Putin said that North Korea’s help in driving Ukrainian forces from the Kursk region of Russia last year “marked a new chapter in the history of military cooperation between our countries.”
Moscow planned to unveil a monument in Kursk by the end of the year to honor the North Korean troops, Mr. Putin said.
During the final meeting of the day, with ASEAN leaders, President Trump told President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines: “I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great. I believe in genetics. They did a good job. You have very good genetics, I can tell you that.”
It was not the first time Mr. Trump has praised the family of Mr. Marcos , who is the son of the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos, who ruled the Philippines for 20 years, imposed martial law and was ousted in 1986.
The only event of substance on President Trump’s schedule today, the signing of a trade deal between the United States and Thailand, did not happen because it was still being finalized. Trump told reporters that “Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on U.S. imports” and that the United States would provide tariff relief, but the two sides signed only a memorandum about the agreement. The president said the deal would be done in the coming weeks.
During an address to Quad leaders, President Trump called Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India, which is a member of the group, “a great leader and a friend of mine, highly respected by everybody all over the world.” The president also praised Modi as he stood with other leaders and took a few questions, calling him a “very tough man.”
India and the United States are navigating a rocky patch in their relationship, largely tied to trade and India’s purchases of Russian oil. Although Modi and Trump signed an interim framework for a trade deal in February, talks have dragged on, frustrating both parties.
The Nvidia turmoil and its implications for the U.S.-China relationship is a backdrop to President Trump’s visit. On Tuesday, shares of technology companies in Asia tumbled after the Trump administration announced rules to restrict overseas access to advanced A.I. chips like those sold by Nvidia. In Hong Kong trading, Alibaba fell 5 percent, while Tencent’s stock dropped nearly 4 percent. The Chinese A.I. firms MiniMax Group fell 7 percent, and Z.AI Co. declined 5 percent.

Russia's growing dependence on China is reshaping one of the world's most important geopolitical relationships. Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the resulting Western sanctions, Russia has relied heavily on Beijing for trade, technology and critical imports. Along the vast Russia-China border, economic cooperation is expanding, but experts warn that the relationship is increasingly unequal, giving China significant leverage.
DW explores historical tensions, Russian security concerns, reports of espionage and the strategic risks facing Russia as China's influence grows, raising questions about the future of the countries' much-publicized "no-limits" partnership.

articles.title_orig: Tracking China’s War of Words Against Japan
articles.title_zh: Tracking China’s War of Words Against Japan
articles.content_orig:
A headline in the Global Times, a newspaper controlled by China’s ruling Communist Party, about Japan’s “remilitarization” after China restricted exports to Japanese entities. Credit... Andy Wong/Associated Press
By Javier C. Hernández and Gal Koplewitz
Javier C. Hernández reported from Tokyo, and Gal Koplewitz from London.
When China’s leader, Xi Jinping, met with President Trump at the White House earlier this fall, the two leaders toasted to friendly relations.
But in private, Mr. Xi offered Mr. Trump a stark warning about Japan, a U.S. ally, according to two officials briefed on the talks, who requested anonymity to discuss private conversations. Mr. Xi told Mr. Trump that Japan’s recent military buildup threatened to destabilize Asia, the officials said, and that Mr. Trump should be cautious about working with Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, describing her as a “militarist.”
The warning from Mr. Xi was part of a broader effort by China to isolate and undermine Japan after Ms. Takaichi said last year that Japan could be forced to defend Taiwan in case of a Chinese invasion. China considers Taiwan, a self-governed democracy that lies just 69 miles from Japan’s westernmost island, part of its territory.
Since the comments, Mr. Xi has overseen a campaign involving propaganda and diplomacy to target Japan, according to interviews with officials and scholars, and an analysis by The New York Times of Chinese Foreign Ministry briefings and state media. It is all part of a push, analysts say, to persuade the world that Japan is a resurgent aggressor.
China has deployed words and images to portray Japan as a World War II-era enemy, using phrases like “remilitarization” and “neo-militarism,” and videos that compare Japan to a “rampaging gray rhino.”
Chinese officials have repeatedly sought to belittle Ms. Takaichi, Japan’s first female prime minister, omitting her title in official briefings, breaking with longstanding practice. State media has depicted Ms. Takaichi in short skirts and a nurse’s uniform in cartoons, and described her as “Abe’s girl,” referring to Shinzo Abe, the former Japanese prime minister and Ms. Takaichi’s mentor.
In private conversations with Western scholars, Chinese academics have recently pushed the narrative that Japan is the “Israel of East Asia,” poised to lead the United States into conflict and destabilize the region.
Russia has helped amplify China’s talking points, branding Japan as a threat. Moscow has echoed Beijing in describing Japan as an “ enemy state ” that is not to be trusted, invoking a World War II-era designation used against former Axis powers.
Mr. Xi and Ms. Takaichi will cross paths this week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit meeting in Shenzhen, China. The encounter is expected to be frosty; Mr. Xi might try to use the summit as an opportunity to alienate Ms. Takaichi from Japan’s allies, experts say.

articles.title_orig: Homebuilder sentiment plunges to 14-year low, leading more builders to drop prices
articles.title_zh: Homebuilder sentiment plunges to 14-year low, leading more builders to drop prices
articles.content_orig:
Sentiment among U.S. homebuilders dropped to the lowest level in 14 years, as higher mortgage rates, higher costs for energy, materials and labor, as well as weaker consumer confidence, led to more builders cutting prices.
Builder confidence in the single-family housing market fell four points to 25, according to the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index, or HMI. That is the lowest since April 2012, when the market was just recovering from the housing crash and foreclosure crisis. Last November, the index stood at 38.
Mortgage rates pulled back slightly in October, but surged higher again last week. The average rate on the 30-year fixed hit 7.51% on Monday, according to Mortgage News Daily. Last year at this time it was 6.38%.
Of the HMI's three components, the index measuring current sales conditions fell six points to 28, and future sales expectations dropped two points to 30. Buyer traffic declined two points to 16 — its lowest level in 15 years, excluding the start of the pandemic in 2020.
"Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today's economy," Bill Owens, NAHB chairman and a home builder and remodeler from Worthington, Ohio, said in a release. "Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction."
More builders are now cutting prices as they try to get buyers in the door. In November, 46% of them  reduced prices, the highest share in the post-Covid period, according to the report. The share of builders using sales incentives also hit a post-Covid high of 68%. That was the 20th consecutive month in which at least 60% of builders used them.
"The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges,  including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability," Robert Dietz, NAHB's chief economist, said in the release. "Mortgage rates above 7%, softer consumer confidence and an uncertain economic outlook are holding buyers back."
In the three-month moving averages for regional HMI scores, the Northeast dropped four points to 34, the Midwest fell five points to 35, the South fell three points to 27, and the West posted a three-point decline to 23.

articles.title_orig: Fed's Cook won't appear at White House hearing on potential firing without changes
articles.title_zh: Fed's Cook won't appear at White House hearing on potential firing without changes
articles.content_orig:
Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook 's attorney on Tuesday gave the strongest signal yet that his client will not attend a hearing at the White House with a "committee of inquiry" investigating mortgage fraud allegations against Cook.
The committee established last month by President Donald Trump , who has previously tried to remove Cook from the central bank's board, is pretextual and poses a threat to the Fed, attorney Abbe Lowell wrote in a letter to presidential counsel Will Scharf.
"Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution's unique status and independence," Lowell wrote in the letter, which is dated Monday and was made public Tuesday.
The latest correspondence came nearly two weeks after the White House committee delayed its proposed hearing with Cook to Dec. 14 from Nov. 5. Lowell said that any hearing with Cook could not take place until at least December because of conflicts with her Fed duties.
While Lowell had raised strong concerns from the outset about the legitimacy of the committee, he initially said Cook "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name."
But he has continued to cast doubts on both the committee's purpose and its composition of three executive branch officials, including National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett .
Lowell's tone sounded more hostile than ever in this week's letter, the first known to be sent by either party in the matter since the Republican Party's devastating losses in the midterm elections on Nov. 3.
He accused Scharf and the committee of seeking "only to manufacture 'cause' for a predetermined removal outcome."
Lowell highlighted two top concerns. First, he asserted that Hassett "is not competent to serve on any factfinding committee" because his prior comments about Cook "demonstrate that he has prejudged the issue."
Second, Lowell called it "fundamentally unfair" that the committee is demanding Cook hand over documents "immediately," while pledging to provide the governor with its own records just seven days before the hearing.
"Your and the Committee's failure to address these legitimate issues, over multiple weeks of back-and-forth correspondence, reinforces my prior observation: President Trump's decision to fire Governor Cook has already been made," Lowell wrote.
"Consequently, this Committee process appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook or to unreasonably manufacture a supposed 'adverse inference' if she does not participate in a process that does not comport with the requirements of a fair hearing," the lawyer wrote.
Lowell told Scharf that Cook would still be prepared to appear for a hearing if the White House "implements fair procedures." But the "ultimatums" Scharf gave in his last reply in early November "do not provide a productive path forward to enabling that participation," Lowell wrote.
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Lowell's letter.
Trump, who frequently urges the Fed to lower interest rates, has long sought to fire Cook, an appointee of former President Joe Biden .
Cook, the first Black woman to serve on the Fed's Board of Governors, last voted to cut rates in December 2025, siding with the majority. The Fed unanimously voted to raise rates after its meeting in September.
Trump officials sent a criminal referral last year alleging Cook may have committed mortgage fraud by falsely claiming different properties as her primary residence in order to get more favorable terms. Cook adamantly denied wrongdoing, and, after Trump tried to fire her in August 2025, filed a lawsuit to block her removal.
The Supreme Court in June prevented Trump from firing Cook, but gave him a path to try again if additional legal steps were taken. In August, the White House told Cook it was reviving its efforts to fire her on mortgage-related grounds. In October, Trump signed a presidential memo establishing the committee of inquiry to investigate allegations that Cook lied on records related to "one or more mortgage instruments."

articles.title_orig: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
articles.title_zh: Trump’s New A.I. Chip Rules Rattle Southeast Asia
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration’s proposal to restrict China’s access to advanced A.I. chips overseas rattled Southeast Asia on Tuesday, threatening a data center investment boom fueled by Chinese companies using the region to sidestep U.S. restrictions on Nvidia’s most powerful chips.
Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Singapore have become offshore computing hubs for Chinese companies such as Alibaba and ByteDance. Data center operators in those countries provide the Chinese firms with remote access to advanced Nvidia chips they cannot buy directly or bring into China.
The strategy has drawn billions of dollars in investment to the region. But in Washington, officials seeking tighter controls on China’s A.I. sector have increasingly viewed data centers as a workaround that poses economic and national security risks.
Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was ousted last week after revelations he had an affair with a woman who formed a Singaporean data center company called Megaspeed. U.S. authorities deemed the woman, Alice Huang, to be an asset for Chinese intelligence services, and they are investigating Megaspeed over allegations of smuggling chips to China. China has denied that Ms. Huang was spying for it.
Separately, Nvidia’s board of directors announced on Tuesday that it had established a committee to oversee “the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.” Nvidia’s board is engaged in a search for a permanent successor to Mr. Huang. The company’s interim chief executive, Colette Kress , is set to preside over the release of the company’s latest quarterly financial results later on Tuesday.
Shares of technology companies tumbled on Tuesday. In trading in Hong Kong, Alibaba fell more than 5 percent, while Tencent’s stock dropped nearly 4 percent. The Chinese A.I. firms MiniMax Group fell more than 7 percent and Z.AI declined more than 5 percent. When markets opened in the United States, tech stocks mostly stabilized from a sell-off the day before, with the Nasdaq index starting the day flat. Nvidia shares faced choppy trading ahead of its earnings results, which are expected after the market closes.

articles.title_orig: California sues OpenAI, alleges it endangered the public by building AI without safeguards
articles.title_zh: California sues OpenAI, alleges it endangered the public by building AI without safeguards
articles.content_orig:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the ChatGPT-maker misled and endangered the public by developing artificial intelligence (AI) models without proper safeguards.
In the lawsuit, Bonta cited the July 2026 attack on the AI platform Hugging Face by experimental OpenAI agents which accessed the internet to breach that company's internal systems.
Bonta claimed OpenAI created a public nuisance and violated the state's unfair competition laws.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the BBC in a statement that Bonta's lawsuit "appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that's been identified by every major AI lab".
Other major AI developers including Anthropic, Meta, and Google have also said their models have staged similar attacks.
But Bonta's lawsuit, filed in San Francisco, where the company is headquartered, appears to be the first such suit filed by a US state.
Hundreds of OpenAI agents coordinated the Hugging Face attack over two days even though they were supposed to be contained in a safe testing environment.
The incident drew added scrutiny because the agents went as far as attempting to cover their tracks.
Bonta announced an investigation into the incident in September, and served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI as part of its probe.
"The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it - this disregard for public safety violated California law," Bonta said in a statement on Monday.
OpenAI said it has been transparent and responsive to the Attorney General's office.
"We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged - and will continue to engage - constructively with the Attorney General's office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry," the company said.
The company added that, since the Hugging Face incident, it has worked to understand and address "misaligned model activity" which industry figures often refer to as rogue agents.
Nathan Calvin, chief strategy officer at AI safety campaign group Encode AI, said the lawsuit "recognises something we at Encode have long raised alarms about".
"OpenAI and other companies developing frontier AI systems have safety and security practices that are insufficient to protect the public from risks that could be catastrophic," he said.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic likely to price IPO above the current range of $70 to $78, sources tell CNBC
articles.title_zh: Anthropic likely to price IPO above the current range of $70 to $78, sources tell CNBC
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic is likely to price its IPO above the current range of $70 to $78, multiple sources told CNBC's David Faber on Tuesday.
The artificial intelligence company is planning to close the order books and lock in total demand at 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Anthropic is slated to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT" and start trading on Nov. 19.
If Anthropic's IPO proceeds as planned, the company will debut roughly five months after SpaceX went public in a record offering that raised $85.7 billion. But Anthropic is facing a public market that's grown increasingly skeptical of the AI trade, as well as mounting and widespread antipathy toward the technology in the U.S.
A group of researchers, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei , co-founded the company in 2021 after defecting from OpenAI , now its chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , and it underwent a period of explosive growth in 2026, driven largely by the popularity of its AI coding tool, Claude Code .
For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year, according to its prospectus . It reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said.
Anthropic has long worked to establish a reputation as a safety-conscious AI company, and its prospectus included more than 90 pages of risk factors for investors to consider ahead of its listing.
"I think if we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia," Amodei said in Anthropic's roadshow video . "We have to make sure that all the risks, all the ways that things can go wrong with this technology, we very carefully address those risks as we bring the benefits and as we have a viable business at the same time."
"I invite you to join us on the next phase of this journey," Amodei said.

articles.title_orig: Sony defeats £2 billion UK claim over PlayStation Store pricing
articles.title_zh: Sony defeats £2 billion UK claim over PlayStation Store pricing
articles.content_orig:
Sony has defeated a major $2.6 billion UK class action lawsuit over the price of PlayStation games.
The lawsuit was brought about by Alex Neill, who is representing consumers that purchased PlayStation digital content between August 2016 and February 2026. The action accused PlayStation of having a ‘near monopoly’ on digital games and add-on content on PlayStation platforms. The case argued that Sony sets strict terms and conditions on developers, and charges a 30% commission on every purchase, which results in “excessive and unfair prices”. It claimed the prices are out of proportion to the costs.
But London’s Competition Appeal Tribunal rejected this, and said the claim failed to establish that PlayStation infringed competition law. As a result, it has dismissed the case in its entirety.
Join The Game Business Today!
The lawsuit argued that once you own a PlayStation, you are trapped within the ecosystem. The Tribunal disagreed, and ruled that Sony competes within a wider ‘systems market’ with the likes of Xbox, Nintendo and PC. It also ruled that gamers can buy physical games (at least for now).
The court said that forcing PlayStation to allow third-party stores onto the platform would be expensive, complex and could impact security. It added that under competition law, there was no legal duty for Sony to do this.
Finally, the court didn’t find pricing to be unfair. It said that Alex Neill had failed to prove Sony’s profit margins were excessive, especially as console makers sell hardware cheaply to make money back on game sales. Furthermore, there tribunal said there no evidence that rival stores would have brought pricing down.
PlayStation still faces similar class actions in Australia, Netherlands and Portugal at an earlier stage.
For more details on the Alex Neill case, you can read our run-down from earlier this year.

articles.title_orig: Windows 11 actually runs better on 8GB of RAM now
articles.title_zh: Windows 11 actually runs better on 8GB of RAM now
articles.content_orig:
I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.
I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.
As recently as the beginning of the year, 16GB of RAM was common on sub-$800 Windows laptops, which helped compensate for an increasingly bloated-feeling Windows 11 . But with the cost of RAM skyrocketing this year, 8GB is once again typical for a starting configuration. The MacBook Neo got away with it, but Windows laptops, including Microsoft’s own 13-inch Surface Laptop , could struggle. Microsoft was talking a big game about making Windows faster and more reliable before the RAM crisis really hit , and it now seems like that effort is beginning to bear fruit .
Earlier this month , Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft’s EVP of Windows and devices, detailed in a blog post the improvements the company has made to Windows 11 to address the constraints of 8GB PCs. In it, Davuluri claims, “Windows is now up to 20% more responsive, and multitasking is up to 40% faster in our lab test.”
The most significant change is in memory management. When there isn’t enough available memory to handle all active data, some of it has to be offloaded (or “paged out”) to storage. And SSDs, especially in lower-cost laptops, are much slower than RAM.
When Windows needs to access data that’s been paged out from the RAM to the SSD, it’s called a hard fault (or page fault). If it happens a lot — say, on a laptop with only 8GB of RAM — it leads to little slowdowns like browser tabs requiring a refresh before you can access them again. Davuluri says, “Windows can now keep up to 2 GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage, so an app or tab you left open is less likely to reload when you return.”
To test this, I fired up the same 13-inch Surface Laptop with 8GB of RAM that I reviewed back in July, when I proclaimed eight is not enough for Windows. This laptop was one of the worst examples of RAMageddon’s current stranglehold on computing: With half the RAM of last year’s base model , it struggled to keep up with my regular workload. And this is Microsoft’s hardware.
Microsoft’s own laptop could struggle
Before updating the Surface to the latest Windows 11 build, I got reacquainted with this laptop and the version of Windows I left it on (25H2, build 26200.8875). It was rough. Running about 20 tabs (on the latest Chrome build) while streaming a 4K YouTube video and using Slack and Signal made everything from clicking tabs to swiping around Windows with trackpad gestures feel sluggish. Chrome tabs and apps would refresh after leaving them in the background for just a short moment. When you’re multitasking and bouncing between many tabs, like when researching something, those refreshes get incredibly frustrating. And the fan was running audibly the whole time. Keeping the Resource Monitor open showed memory hard faults ranging from just under 700 faults per second to 29,000 faults per second, during which Windows ground to a halt. Seeing this number literally go off its chart showed just how badly Windows 11 struggled with memory management on 8GB before the update.
Now, after updating the Surface Laptop to Windows 11 version 26H2, build 26300.9974 ( memory improvements are live on build 26300.9818 and beyond) things are much improved. I opened over 30 Chrome tabs while streaming the same 4K YouTube video and running the same chat apps, and Windows slowed a bit, but nowhere near as much. I could feel things like Task View get a little less responsive and at times stuttery, but it was the way you’d expect when taxing a system. Chrome tabs required less frequent refreshes. The fan also took longer to kick in and ran a little quieter and for shorter durations when it did.
Taking a fresh look at the Resource Monitor, hard faults at normal operation were now under 300 per second, with occasional jumps to about 1,000. Performance was even slightly better when I subbed out Chrome for Microsoft Edge. Edge felt more responsive under load and had fewer hard faults when running 30 tabs, the same 4K YouTube video, and a Google Meet video call.
I’m happy to see that the 8GB Surface Laptop now performs better, and I’m equally relieved that Windows 11 is starting to feel more viable on 8GB of RAM. (It’s still a shame the 8GB Surface Laptop costs more than last year’s 16GB, but I digress.) Do I want 8GB of RAM in any laptop I’m personally buying? No.
As I said when I reviewed the latest Dell XPS 13 , I appreciate that 8GB is workable — and it should be fine for basic needs today — but I still advise getting 16GB if you’re able. The extra headroom will keep things speedy for longer, especially after you bog a computer down with lots of files, apps, or games. And as much better as the 8GB Surface Laptop is now, I still managed to crash Chrome entirely with fewer than three dozen tabs. Microsoft has done better by its entry-level laptop, but it’s not a miracle worker.
Our ongoing RAMageddon makes living with lower quantities of memory a grim reality. Microsoft is partly to blame for that, of course. And it hasn’t done itself any favors with all the feature bloat it put into Windows 11 during the Copilot / AI era . Meanwhile, other OSes, like Linux, macOS, and ChromeOS, can get by better with less. Still, I’m glad to see Microsoft ever so slightly right the ship in this one way.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia shares set for $335 billion swing after earnings, options show
articles.title_zh: Nvidia shares set for $335 billion swing after earnings, options show
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia reports Tuesday with its longtime finance chief, Colette Kress , in charge. The Bank of Nvidia she inherited was already turning customers away.
Wall Street will grade Nvidia ( NVDA ) on chips and guidance after the bell . But the most revealing page may sit in the back of the filing, where Nvidia lists what it has promised to pay or guarantee for others.
That list nearly doubled in a single quarter, JPMorgan's Michael Cembalest noted , and comes to about $530 billion with guarantees included. Huang's exit put that web of deals under the microscope.
The man who built the bank had already started closing its windows.
In August, Nvidia's guarantee for OpenAI's Ohio data center came in at less than half the $250 billion that had been discussed. By the end of the month, Nvidia had paused revenue-sharing deals with neoclouds — upstart cloud companies that rent out Nvidia chips — The Wall Street Journal reported . In October, Huang told those partners to get their customers to pay upfront.
"You're not charging what you should be charging," he told them at a conference in Berlin, according to the Journal.
Neoclouds may be rooting for a Huang comeback , but his return wouldn't reopen windows he was shutting himself. Kress is expected to tighten the purse strings even further, the Journal reported. The $500 billion lending platform Nvidia launched with Wall Street in August still hasn't closed a deal, and lenders want Nvidia to back more than a quarter of each loan, Bloomberg reported.
"I do expect the company to pivot pretty hard under new leadership," Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management, said on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang. "I think we're going to see less circular financing activity. We've already seen a slowdown just in the last three weeks."
The stock market noticed first. CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and Nebius ( NBIS ) have each lost more than half their value in three months, while Nvidia is down about 30%. Nebius is still up for the year.
Some promises can't be taken back. Deals Nvidia already signed — from chip supply orders to cloud capacity it agreed to rent back — are still owed. And Nvidia is set to buy $10 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the AI lab's IPO , which prices Wednesday, according to Anthropic's amended filing.
That makes Tuesday's report about more than demand. Investors will want to know whether the pile of promises keeps growing, and whether Kress sounds like a banker who's still lending.
David Nelson, chief strategist at Belpointe Asset Management, sees two AI trades hiding inside one. Some companies pay for their data centers out of the cash they earn. Others lean on leases, loan guarantees and "other people's money," as he put it, the kind of help Nvidia has been handing out.
"They have been priced as one trade," he wrote Monday. "They won't be much longer."

articles.content_orig:
Deutsche Bank’s headquarters in Frankfurt. The bank long resisted breaking with Russia’s most important business titans under President Vladimir V. Putin. Credit... Felix Schmitt for The New York Times
By Russ Buettner Khadija Sharife Brian Fitzpatrick Frederik Obermaier Bastian Obermayer and Sophia Baumann
When Russian missiles began pummeling Ukraine in February 2022, executives at one of the world’s largest banks sensed trouble headed their way.
Within hours of an invasion that set off a war that is now in its fifth year, Western governments issued new financial sanctions intended to further isolate Russia from the world economy.
At Deutsche Bank, a longtime bank of Russian industry titans and oligarchs, officials scrambled to get ahead of the damage. “Russian Sanctions Urgent Request” read the subject line of an email sent by one of Deutsche’s anti-financial crime specialists to her colleagues.
“As you know we have a large Russian Oligarchs client population” and other clients with investments in Russian companies, she wrote. She asked which of those clients “we potentially could unwind and which not.” Should the bank advise them, she wondered, to withdraw their money “while they still can?”
This email exchange was the beginning of a frenzied reckoning within the scandal-plagued bank over its long resistance to breaking with Russia’s most important business titans under Vladimir V. Putin, the Russian president. The bank’s clients included the Russian billionaires Oleg V. Deripaska and Viktor F. Vekselberg. Time and again over many years, records show, Deutsche Bank’s risk managers warned that such relationships were perilous.
But profits associated with maintaining its Russian clients won out every time.
Russia’s war in Ukraine swept up Deutsche Bank in a larger shift. For decades, German politicians and business leaders believed that working with Russia and deepening economic ties between the two countries would discourage Russian aggression. That strategy collapsed after the invasion.

articles.title_orig: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
articles.title_zh: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
articles.content_orig:
The UK has sanctioned companies it said are involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, in the first package of measures since the government announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the territory.
The government said the sanctions against eight construction and property development firms would disrupt their flows of finance and ability to support building in the West Bank.
The construction of settlements, which are illegal under international law, has risen sharply in recent years.
There has also been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property.
Israel is yet to comment on the announcement, but has previously condemned UK sanctions related to West Bank settlements, accusing the Labour government of "systematically acting against the State of Israel".
However, the Palestinian foreign ministry welcomed the UK's move.
It comes two days before the deadline for bids for construction tenders in the highly sensitive E1 area east of Jerusalem.
The plans, which have been condemned internationally, would in effect divide the West Bank in two and cut it off from East Jerusalem.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the E1 development would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine".
The sanctions also target Tzav 9, an Israeli activist movement which the UK government says has organised and carried out blockades to prevent aid entering Gaza.
It comes after the UK expanded its human rights sanctions regime last month, enabling the government to sanction individuals and companies involved in violations of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world.
The government is also developing separate legislation to ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements and the provision of advertising services for settlement properties in the UK.
Miliband said: "Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this government's approach.
"That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.
"The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable.
"We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike."
In September, the UK government announced that it would ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements, as well as acting against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.
At the time, Miliband said the move marked the beginning of a "new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which "not only calls out injustice and suffering, but acts".
That announcement prompted a furious reaction from Israel , which said it would shut the British consulate in East Jerusalem in retaliation.
Last month, most diplomats left the consulate - which handled UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza - but the UK insisted that the building would not be closing and would operate as a "UK mission".
Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.
There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.
